name: rule-engine
intent: Keep decision logic in an explicit, versionable rule base - condition-action rules that an engine matches against a working memory of facts - so the rules can change without editing or redeploying the code that uses them.
problem: Decision logic that changes on a faster rhythm than the surrounding code (pricing tiers, eligibility, scoring, entitlements, routing) is scattered through nested conditionals inside services, so every policy change touches compiled code, needs a release, and cannot be reviewed by the people who own the rule.
context: Fits component/module level and request or message flows where the rule count is small enough to be read as a list but too volatile to hard-code: business policy owned by domain experts, per-tenant or per-region variations, and decisions over facts assembled from several sources. Staying debuggable requires an explicit execution model - declared conflict resolution, bounded chaining, traceable firings - because the pattern replaces the call stack with a rule base.
benefits: Rule changes become data changes: a policy update ships as a new rule set, without recompiling the host and often without a deploy.
Rules are declarative and reviewable by domain experts: a condition-action list can be read, diffed and audited by the people who own the policy.
Conditions and actions become reusable building blocks: the same fact vocabulary and operator set serve many rules, and compound policy is composed from rules instead of nested inside one.
Evaluation is explainable: a run can report which rules matched with which facts, which is what audits and incident debugging need and what a compiled if-chain cannot provide.
The decision surface is separately testable: rules are data, so scenario tables can be replayed against the rule base without starting the application.
Rule sets can be swapped per tenant, region or version, so one engine serves several policies concurrently.
tradeoffs: A second program to own: the rule base, its format, its loader and its tests have their own lifecycle, versioning and review process, and they drift from the code's types unless something validates them.

Implicit control flow: which rule fires and in what order is decided by the engine's agenda and conflict resolution rather than by the call stack, so behaviour cannot be understood by reading one function top to bottom.

Emergent behaviour: rule interaction, chaining and rules that re-assert the facts they matched can produce cascades or non-convergence; engines bound this with refraction, no-loop flags or iteration caps, not by construction.

No compile-time checking: conditions in strings or data are resolved at run time, so a renamed field, a typo'd fact id or an unknown operator shows up as a runtime error or a silently false condition.
Runtime cost: matching consumes time and memory (indexes or Rete memories, agenda and session state) and the engine must be instantiated per evaluation - overhead a compiled conditional never had.

Externalized rules are an audit and attack surface: whoever can write rule data changes production behaviour, and expression languages that can call methods or reach the environment are equivalent to remote code execution.

participants.responsibility: Condition-action pair as data: the left-hand side (condition) matches facts, the right-hand side (action/consequence) is what happens when it matches.
Holds the rule set that is loaded, versioned and evaluated together - the unit that policy owners edit, review and deploy.
The data the rules reason over; facts are asserted, modified or retracted, and those changes drive re-evaluation.
Determines which rules' conditions currently match the facts, using indexing or a discrimination network (Rete) instead of re-evaluating every rule against every fact.
Orders the activated rules and picks the next one to fire deterministically (salience, recency, specificity or declared rule order).
Owns the working memory for one evaluation (a request, message or job), inserts facts, triggers firing and is discarded afterwards.
Reads rule definitions from their store (files, database, DSL text, JSON), validates them and turns them into the engine's internal form.

use_cases: Pricing, discount and promotion engines where tiers, thresholds and eligibility are edited per campaign or per market.
Fraud, credit and risk scoring over transactions or events, where facts are asserted and re-evaluated as new signals arrive.
Entitlement, access and compliance policy: which action a subject may perform on a resource under current conditions, kept readable for auditors.
Routing and approval workflows whose conditions and thresholds are business-owned (claims triage, support escalation, document review queues).
Diagnostics and alerting over telemetry, where threshold and correlation rules replace hand-coded alerting branches.

Policy-as-code engines: Open Policy Agent evaluates Rego rules - declarative condition rules over JSON input - for admission control, API authorization and infrastructure policy, with the decision offloaded from the service to the engine.

Microsoft's open-source RulesEngine (.NET) evaluates JSON-defined rule workflows (RuleName + Expression per rule) loaded from external stores (files, SQL, Cosmos) at runtime, returning a per-rule result tree for pricing-style discount policies.

Prometheus alerting rules are a scheduled rule base: each rule is a PromQL condition (expr) plus a for-duration, evaluated every group interval against current series, with labels and annotations as the action's output.
avoid_when: There are only a handful of stable conditions: ordinary if/else - or the Specification pattern when the rules must be composable objects - is clearer and faster.
The logic is a sequence of steps with side effects and explicit ordering: that is a workflow or a plain procedure, not a rule base.
Conditions must be type-checked, exhaustively matched and refactor-safe at compile time: sealed hierarchies with exhaustive matching, or Strategy implementations, give the compiler that job.
One evaluation per object with no cross-fact matching and a hard latency budget: a compiled predicate is cheaper than any engine, and a rule table of closures is enough.
Rules would come from untrusted authors, or the expression language can reach the environment: externalized rules then become an execution surface rather than configuration.
anti_patterns: Rule base as a general-purpose language: loops, sequencing and orchestration encoded as rules until the policy store is an untyped, untested program.
Salience as control flow: ordering rules by priority numbers instead of modelling precedence, so nobody can predict the firing order without running it.
Rules that mutate what they match: an action re-asserts the fact its own condition tested and the rule fires again until the engine hits an iteration cap.
Untyped rule stores: rule text or JSON edited directly in production with no schema validation, versioning, review or replay tests.
Reinventing the pattern on top of a full engine - or buying a Rete engine for three rules: either duplicate agenda/matching logic in application code or pay for infrastructure nobody needs.
design_principles: Separation of policy from mechanism: the decisions are data, the engine is the mechanism.
Open/closed principle: new rules extend behaviour without modifying the code that runs them.
Single responsibility per rule: one condition, one decision - compound policy is composed from rules, not nested inside one.
Explicit over implicit: declare conflict resolution, chaining and revision semantics instead of relying on rule order.
Testability as a design constraint: rules must be expressible as data so scenario tables can be replayed - which makes testing more important, not less.
best_practices: Keep the rule base small and its context narrow; an engine that indexes thousands of rules solves a performance problem you should not have created (limit chaining, or eliminate it).
Make evaluation deterministic: declare the conflict-resolution policy, refuse salience tuning as a substitute for modelling, and report which rule won.
Keep conditions side-effect free and make every action state which facts it changes (modify/update, retract) so re-evaluation terminates.
Validate, version and review the rule store like source code: schema-check on load, fail fast on unknown fields/operators, keep diffs and a replay suite of scenarios.
Trace which rules fired with which facts for every evaluation; explainability is the operational payoff and the first thing missing during an incident.
Prefer the lightest realization that fits: an in-process table of predicates before a full Rete engine or a bought BRMS.
sources: Martin Fowler, RulesEngine (bliki, 2009) and the DSL catalog entry Production Rule System - a rule set is a condition-action list evaluated over working memory; the article warns that rule interaction is the maintenance dragon and that a hand-rolled, narrow engine often beats a product.
Drools/KIE documentation - production memory, working memory, agenda, conflict resolution, truth maintenance and forward/backward chaining define the canonical vocabulary of this pattern.
CLIPS Basic Programming Guide 6.4.2 (NASA Johnson Space Center) - defrule, fact-list, agenda, salience, refraction: the production rule model in a C implementation.
